name: Eval-in-production: spot the mistake
note: Three reasonable-sounding moves for evaluating quality on live traffic. Pick the flaw before the chapter names it — each maps to sampling, significance, or what you sample.

items.prompt: To never miss a regression, we'll run the full LLM judge on 100% of production traffic and alert on any quality drop.
candidates: Scoring every request doubles your inference bill (a judge call per query) for little gain — sample a fraction, sized so you can still detect a regression of the magnitude you care about
Judges are too unreliable to run in production at all
100% is fine; the real problem is you should alert on latency too
You should only evaluate traffic that users complain about
items.correct: Scoring every request doubles your inference bill (a judge call per query) for little gain — sample a fraction, sized so you can still detect a regression of the magnitude you care about
items.explanation: Eval-in-prod is sampling: a judge call costs roughly what the original call did, so 100% coverage doubles spend (Chapter 4). You don't need it — a sampled few-hundred-per-day is enough to detect a meaningful drop. The sampling rate is a detection-speed-vs-cost dial, not an all-or-nothing switch.
items.principle: You evaluate a sample of live traffic, not all of it; the rate trades detection speed against spend.

items.prompt: Sampled prod accuracy went from 0.94 last week to 0.91 this week, measured on 40 sampled queries each. Roll back the release.
candidates: A 3-point move on 40 samples is well within sampling noise — gate on whether the paired difference's confidence interval excludes zero, not on the point estimate, or you'll roll back on coin flips
Roll back immediately; any drop in accuracy is unacceptable
Ignore it — accuracy always fluctuates and never matters
Raise the guardrail to 0.91 so the alert stops firing
items.correct: A 3-point move on 40 samples is well within sampling noise — gate on whether the paired difference's confidence interval excludes zero, not on the point estimate, or you'll roll back on coin flips
items.explanation: Because you sampled, the measured accuracy is an estimate with error bars. On 40 examples a 3-point swing easily straddles zero — rolling back on it means thrashing on noise. The gate is a significance test (a bootstrap CI on the paired difference, as in the Evaluation guide): block only when the regression survives the noise. The fix for a genuinely ambiguous signal is a bigger sample, not a hair-trigger.
items.principle: Gate on the confidence interval, not the point estimate — a drop must beat sampling noise to count.

items.prompt: We sample traffic uniformly and score it with an LLM judge. The aggregate quality number looks healthy, but a specific user segment keeps complaining.
candidates: Uniform sampling drowns a small hard segment in the easy majority, so its failures never move the aggregate — stratify the sample by segment, and validate the judge against human labels so it's scoring the thing that's failing
The complaining users are wrong; the aggregate number is the truth
LLM judges can't be trusted, so ignore the eval entirely
Just increase the overall sampling rate and the problem will surface
items.correct: Uniform sampling drowns a small hard segment in the easy majority, so its failures never move the aggregate — stratify the sample by segment, and validate the judge against human labels so it's scoring the thing that's failing
items.explanation: A healthy aggregate can hide a failing slice: if 3% of traffic is a hard segment, even a total failure there barely dents the overall mean. Stratified sampling (guarantee coverage of segments you care about) plus a judge you've checked against human labels is how eval-in-prod sees the failure the average smooths away. Raising the uniform rate just collects more of the easy majority.
items.principle: A healthy average can hide a failing slice — stratify the sample, and trust the judge only after you've validated it.
